newsitem.title: USA: NYS comptroller to review Swiss bank ban on merit.
newsitem.headline: NYS comptroller to review Swiss bank ban on merit.

text.p: New York State will review a ban on investing its extra cash with Swiss banks, put in place until probes of how the banks treated Holocaust victims end, as warranted, the comptroller's spokesman said Friday.

Dennis Tompkins, a spokesman for Comptroller H. Carl McCall, explained the prohibition, which went into effect on January 30, was never intended to be permanent. "When we made the decision, we obviously made it pending further review and discussion. Yes, we will reassess this as things progress."

The spokesman was reacting to a statement by a spokeswoman for the World Jewish Congress, who said that McCall would reconsider his decision after a meeting between representatives of the comptroller and the congress on Friday.

The announcement that the New York State comptroller had stopped using Swiss banks for short-term investments caught the banks by surprise as it came on the heels of a decision by the country's three biggest banks to defuse the emotional issue of what happened to wartime Jewish bank accounts by setting up a $70 million memorial fund for Holocaust victims.

What benchmarks the Swiss banks would have to meet to persuade the New York State comptroller to lift the ban or the likely timing of any decision to do so were subjects that were too speculative to discuss, his spokesman said.

McCall will be testifying at a hearing in New York City on February 13 that will be held by Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver into the "current process for regulating foreign banks," as they are allowed under state law to take municipal deposits and public pension fund investments. He also is expected to meet that week with Jewish organizations who represent Holocaust victims.

The comptroller's office since August has been assisting Jewish organizations in tracing dormant accounts, Tompkins added. Banks in New York State turn dormant accounts over to the comptroller after five years, and there are concerns that some of the funds Holocaust victims deposited in Swiss banks were sent to New York during World War Two for safekeeping.
